question: How do you power and cool a rack that draws 130 kW?
title: Data Center Infrastructure: A Practical Reference
lede: A decade of data center design assumed 5–10 kW racks and air. AI training racks draw 80–140 kW and are heading past 250, which breaks the air assumption, the power assumption, and usually the building. This guide catalogs {{N_ENTRIES}} systems across seven classes, with the rack density each one actually supports, how much water it uses, and whether it can go into a hall that already exists.

facets.label: Density
facets.tip: Rack power density the system can support. Low under 10 kW/rack is legacy enterprise · Medium 10–40 kW covers most cloud racks · High 40–100 kW is where air stops working · Extreme above 100 kW is AI training. Most systems span a band, and the top of that band is what matters.

facets.label: Used in
facets.tip: Where the system is normally deployed. AI training is called out separately from hyperscale because its density, power ramp rate, and cooling requirements differ enough to change the design.

facets.label: Water use
facets.tip: On-site water consumption when the system is running. This is the metric communities and regulators ask about, and it trades directly against electricity: evaporative cooling saves power and spends water, closed loops do the reverse. Untagged where the system does not touch the water balance.

facets.label: Retrofit
facets.tip: How disruptive the system is to install in a facility that already exists. Drop-in = goes into a live hall rack by rack · Hall retrofit = needs a room taken out of service and reworked · New build = the building has to be designed around it.

facets.label: Maturity
facets.tip: Mature = standard practice with many suppliers · Established = commercial and widely deployed but newer · Emerging = shipping at scale only in the last few years · Early = deployed in pilots and single sites.
